value.overview: The Whistling Heron is a medium-sized heron of tropical and subtropical South America. Unlike many herons, it often feeds on land rather than in deep water, walking through grasslands, wet fields, savannas, and lightly wooded areas. Its contrasting gray, buff, yellow, black, and pink coloration makes it distinctive. The species is the only member of the genus Syrigma and is known for clear whistling calls and a generally deliberate, terrestrial feeding style.
value.classification: The Whistling Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae. Two subspecies are generally recognized: Syrigma sibilatrix fostersmithi in northern South America and the nominate S. s. sibilatrix farther south and east.
value.identification: This heron is about 50–58 centimeters long and has a gray body and wings, a yellowish-gold neck and upper breast, and dark crest feathers. The face shows blue skin around the lores, while the large bill is pinkish with a black tip. The legs are dark. In flight, buff or pale wing edges can be noticeable. Its upright posture, long legs, terrestrial habits, and distinctive whistled calls help separate it from other herons.
value.rangeHabitat: The main range extends from Colombia and Venezuela south and east through Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, Uruguay, and northern Argentina. It uses wet savannas, marshy grasslands, rice fields, muddy margins, shallow wetlands, drainage ditches, rural areas, and open landscapes with scattered trees or woodland remnants. In Costa Rica it is an exceptionally rare accidental visitor rather than an established species. The first documented national record was an individual observed foraging at Manzanillo, Limón Province, on February 16, 2016, representing the northernmost documented record at that time.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident within its South American range, with local movements and dispersal rather than a well-defined long-distance migration. In Costa Rica it is known from rare accidental occurrence, and there is no reliable evidence that it has established a resident or regular migratory population.
value.breeding: Whistling Herons usually nest in mature trees, including trees in small woodlots, forest remnants, and open rural landscapes. The nest is a loose platform of sticks, commonly placed on a substantial horizontal branch several meters above the ground. They generally breed alone or in small, scattered groups. Clutches usually contain three or four pale blue, speckled eggs. Incubation lasts about 28 days, and young remain associated with adults after leaving the nest.
value.dietFeeding: The species takes a broad variety of small animals, especially insects such as grasshoppers, dragonflies, beetles, and mantises. It also eats earthworms, spiders, crustaceans, frogs, small reptiles, and other small vertebrates when available. It commonly forages in grasslands and shallow wet places, walking slowly and pausing upright before making a quick stab or lunge. Individuals may feed alone or in pairs.
value.behavior: Whistling Herons are often active during daylight and spend considerable time on the ground. They walk slowly through open habitat, sometimes making short runs or catching flying insects. Birds may perch or roost in trees and can tolerate relatively open, human-modified landscapes. They are usually solitary or found in pairs, though larger gatherings may occur at roosts. Communication includes clear whistles and hissing sounds, particularly in family groups.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, and the species is locally common to abundant in parts of its South American range. Its occurrence in Costa Rica is too rare and recent to support a separate national population assessment.
